units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, Ben. What is Brussels now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On paper, it's the Brussels-Capital Region, a territory of nineteen municipalities with about one and a quarter million people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The City of Brussels, the historic center with the Grand Place, is only one of those nineteen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The others have their own mayors and councils.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And names that Brusselers use as proudly as the name of the city itself: Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, Schaerbeek, Anderlecht, Molenbeek, Uccle, and more.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The region is the capital of Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the capital of the Flemish Community and of the French Community.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it is, informally but unmistakably, the capital of Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The governance is a puzzle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Belgium is a federation of three regions and three language communities, layered on top of each other, and Brussels sits at the point where they all overlap.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The region's parliament has French-speaking and Dutch-speaking groups, and the government has to include members of both.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That sounds like a clever safeguard, and it is.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It also makes things slow.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Very slow, recently.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After regional elections in June of 2024, the parties couldn't agree on a coalition.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It took 613 days, more than twenty months, until a seven-party government finally took office in February of 2026, led by a French-speaking liberal, Boris Dilliès.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The parties had to promise to balance a budget that was deeply in deficit, and to merge various regional agencies.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So for almost two years the capital of Europe ran on a caretaker government.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did. And at the national level, the story has been similar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After elections in June of 2024, it took more than two hundred thirty days for a federal government to form.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In February of 2025, Bart De Wever, a Flemish nationalist who had long dreamed of a more independent Flanders, was sworn in as prime minister by King Philippe, in a five-party coalition.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which is an irony.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the first time a Flemish nationalist had led the Belgian government, the kind of irony Belgian history delivers regularly.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King Philippe, who succeeded his father Albert the Second in 2013, is the seventh king of the Belgians.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the real face of modern Brussels is its people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the first of January, 2025, the region counted about one million, two hundred fifty-six thousand people, and a bit over thirty-seven percent of them held a foreign passport.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's not counting the many Belgians with a foreign background.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Residents come from about a hundred and eighty-three different nationalities.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who are the biggest groups?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The largest foreign group is French, followed by Romanians and Italians, then Spaniards and Moroccans.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels also has an important Congolese community, centered on a district called Matongé.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 2025, for the first time since the mid-nineteen-nineties, the population stopped growing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Many of those foreign residents work for the institutions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The European Commission, the Council of the European Union, and parts of the European Parliament all have their seats here, around the Schuman roundabout and the Rue de la Loi.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: NATO's headquarters, rebuilt in a striking new complex in the north of the city and opened in 2018, is in Brussels too.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How many people work for international institutions?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the most recent count, more than fifty thousand in the region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around them are embassies, trade associations, law firms, think tanks, and the lobbyists who try to influence the laws of the European Union.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A city that once lived by cloth and tapestries now lives largely by words and rules.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It hasn't all been easy, though.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The city has had dark days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In November of 2015, after the terror attacks in Paris, some of whose planners had lived in the Brussels district of Molenbeek, the city went into a security lockdown that lasted days, with soldiers on the streets and the metro closed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then, on the eighteenth of March, 2016, police captured one of the key suspects, Salah Abdeslam, in Molenbeek.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And four days later.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the morning of the twenty-second of March, three suicide bombers struck.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two bombs exploded in the departure hall of Brussels Airport at Zaventem, and an hour later, a third went off on a metro train leaving the Maalbeek station, in the heart of the European Quarter, right among the offices of the institutions.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How many people were killed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Thirty-two people, not counting the attackers, and more than three hundred were injured.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Islamic State group claimed responsibility.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every year since, the city has marked the anniversary, and the little statue of the Manneken Pis has been dressed in a firefighter's uniform to honor the rescuers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the city has been rethinking how it lives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2015, the central boulevards around the Bourse were closed to cars, creating one of the largest pedestrian zones in Europe, and the old Boulevard Anspach, once built over the buried Senne, became a place for people to walk and sit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A low-emission zone limits older cars, and a traffic plan called Good Move, which reduces through traffic in residential neighborhoods, has been bitterly debated.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Like most such efforts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is trying to become a city for people rather than just for commuters, and, like most such efforts, it's argued over fiercely.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's the culture, which is as eclectic as the population.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is the capital of the comic strip, with dozens of giant murals of comic heroes painted on building walls across the city, a museum devoted to the art form, and a tradition that gave the world Tintin and the Smurfs.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And beer and chocolate.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2016, UNESCO recognized Belgian beer culture as part of the world's cultural heritage.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And according to tradition, the praline, the filled chocolate, was invented in 1912 by a Brussels chocolatier named Jean Neuhaus, in the elegant glass-roofed Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert, one of the oldest covered shopping arcades in Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Waffles, fries, mussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a small green vegetable that carries the city's name, the Brussels sprout, which was grown in the area around the city centuries ago.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The city is also reckoning with its past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Royal Museum for Central Africa, in Tervuren, which Leopold the Second built as a showcase of his colony, was closed for years and reopened in 2018 after a major renovation that tried to confront its colonial origins.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2020, during worldwide protests against racism, statues of Leopold the Second in Belgium were defaced, and some were removed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the royal apology.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A parliamentary commission examined Belgium's colonial past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2022, King Philippe visited the Democratic Republic of the Congo and expressed deep regret for the suffering caused by colonial rule.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The debate is ongoing, and it will shape how the city understands itself in the years ahead.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If you had to pick a symbol for Brussels, what would it be?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not a lion or a saint or a king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A dog. In the local dialect, a zinneke is a mongrel, a mixed-breed street dog that belongs to no one breed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brusselers use the word with affection.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For their city, a place of mixed languages, mixed origins, and mixed styles, where no one is quite purebred.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a small bronze statue of a dog, relieving itself against a post, on a street in the old center, and a colorful parade, held every two years, that celebrates the zinneke spirit.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So let's step back and look at the whole journey.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It began as a settlement in a marsh, with a chapel on an island.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a market town on the road between Flanders and Cologne, and a ducal capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its guilds won a seat at the table.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It became the capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, the home of great painters and weavers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was nearly erased in 1695, and rebuilt in four years into one of the most beautiful squares in the world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It passed from Spain to Austria to France to the Dutch, and in 1830, after a night at the opera and four days of street fighting, it became the capital of a new nation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It grew rich under Leopold, on the profits of an empire built on terrible cruelty.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was occupied twice, and spared the worst of two world wars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And then, almost by accident, it became the working capital of a united Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Through all of it, Brussels has been a place where different peoples and languages meet, argue, trade, and build together.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It has never had one identity, and perhaps that is its identity.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That is the story of Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Thank you for listening.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And enjoy the city.
